OpenAI andGoogle Cloud⁠(opens in a new window)are partnering to bring OpenAI’s frontier models andCodex⁠(opens in a new window)agentic workflows into Google Cloud’s Model Garden. The integration will give customers native access to these models to power complex agentic workflows at scale, backed by Google Cloud’s data governance and high-performance infrastructure.

Google Cloud’s longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them. Bringing OpenAI models to its model garden gives these teams access to OpenAI’s frontier models within the environment where they already work, enabling enterprises to modernize their software development lifecycle, build agentic workflows, and change how people work.

For organizations in regulated industries, deploying AI requires control over who can access sensitive data and how it is used. The integration will pair OpenAI’s frontier models with Google Cloud’s built-in access controls, centralized data governance, and high-performance infrastructure to support demanding enterprise workloads.

Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI frontier models via model garden, transacted through the Google Cloud Marketplace. Enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments will be able to draw down their GCP commitments for these purchases.

Additionally, OpenAI models will soon be available in Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent, providing enterprise customers with model choice flexibility and the best model for each task. By expanding access through Google Cloud, we are giving enterprises greater choice in how they discover and use frontier models, with a path from evaluation to broader adoption.

General availability is planned in the coming weeks. Request access to OpenAI on Google Cloudhere.

Microsoft remains OpenAI’s primary cloud partner.

Google Antigravity와 Gemini Agent에도 OpenAI 모델을 제공할 계획이며, 정식 출시는 수주 내로 예고됐다. 기업의 모델 선택권과 기존 클라우드 환경 내 에이전트 도입 경로를 넓히는 변화지만, Microsoft는 여전히 OpenAI의 주력 클라우드 파트너다.

articles.title: Security
articles.content:
October 21, 2026

Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run websites and web applications. Calif identified a critical flaw using GPT‑5.6 Sol as part of ourPatch the Planet⁠(opens in a new window)initiative, with Wiz also independently discovering and reporting both vulnerabilities. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with our teams and partners like Wiz, Cloudflare, and others contributing research, technical support, and coordination to prepare protections ahead of disclosure.

For organizations using PHP, the priority now is applying the fixes.We’re sharing a PHP version checker as a Codex skill⁠(opens in a new window)to help operators identify potentially vulnerable PHP versions and, alongside PHP’s and their providers’ guidance, determine which updates apply.

Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory. It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.

To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did, opening aDefender’s Windowfor maintainers and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure.

To help more defenders use these capabilities, we’ve committed $1 billion in subsidizedDaybreak accessthroughDaybreak for Frontline Defenders, focused on organizations with limited security resources protecting essential services.

As significant as they are, these bugs are among several significant vulnerabilities we’ve already found and are working to fix, and we expect similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months. Drawing on our experience thus far, we’re sharing a proposed approach, appropriate for the AI era, to responding to critical vulnerabilities in widely used software, and we’re asking the security community to help improve this framework. It brings together our models, security expertise, and maintainers to help turn findings into protection and build a response that can scale as AI capabilities advance.

Getting a fix into use can mean adapting it for older releases, preparing provider mitigations, and updating systems across many organizations. A repeatable process helps those teams act quickly as more vulnerabilities are discovered.

Through Patch the Planet, we contributed security expertise and model access to support the PHP response, and worked with maintainers and research partners to test fixes and prepare guidance. We also helped coordinate with infrastructure providers on protections for affected systems and engaged government cyber agencies to help guidance reach critical organizations. This supported the maintainer-led response and helped other defenders prepare.

For some findings, researchers can work directly with the software’s maintainers to investigate the issue and develop a fix. Others need a wider response because they affect many products or because distributors and service providers need time (which may be in short supply if frontier capabilities are not too far ahead of those that are broadly available) to prepare updates and protections. In those cases, the proposed framework can help maintainers identify who needs to be involved and coordinate the work. The response can involve five stages:

Validate and fix the upstream vulnerability.The maintainer, researchers, and essential technical partners confirm the finding, assess its impact, and develop and test a fix. This process includes adversarial testing with frontier models to look for ways around the patch and related variants of the vulnerability.

Give affected organizations time to act.We propose a framework for considering which organizations need advance information to prepare protections, while maintainers decide whom to involve. We help with outreach, information-sharing agreements, and coordination between teams. A distributor might adapt a fix for an older release, a hosting provider might test a mitigation, and a security provider might prepare detection or prevention measures, including web application firewall (WAF) rules.

Coordinate with government partners to help protect critical systems.Government agencies play an essential role in coordinating a wider response and helping security guidance reach organizations responsible for critical infrastructure and other essential services. In the case of PHP, we worked, in collaboration with our partners, to engage with multiple parts of the U.S. government, including the White House’s Super Intelligence Force, the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), as well as international partners to support that effort.

Prepare updates across affected products.As the fix, guidance, and disclosure plans become stable, maintainers can involve additional distributors, hosting and service providers, response teams, and operators to prepare updates and address gaps in coverage.

Once a patch is available, publish guidance and support deployment.Public guidance helps people assess their exposure, find authoritative updates or interim mitigations, and check that a fix is running. The response continues as operators deploy updates and report where they need help.

The proposed framework considers an organization’s protective role, including protecting its own systems and customers, the time needed to act, and its ability to handle sensitive information. The same criteria would apply to comparable organizations, with maintainers deciding whom to involve ahead of disclosure.

Each participant receives the information needed to carry out their protective work, from network logs with indicators of compromise to more sensitive working proof-of-concept exploits. Even limited details can reveal a vulnerability, so we weigh the risk of sharing them against the protection they enable.

Teams following this framework would work with maintainers to give defenders time to prepare and reassess the timeline if there’s active exploitation in the wild, a leak, a revealing public patch, or increased risk to users from stalled remediation.

ThePatch the Planet website⁠(opens in a new window)brings together public disclosures and guidance to help operators identify affected systems, find the right update, and verify that the updated software is running properly. For PHP, it points to the maintainers’ official patch and upgrade instructions and our partners’ technical research. The guidance also covers interim mitigations, when to involve a provider or expert, and backup and recovery. Interim protections can reduce risk, but we’ll make their limits and operational tradeoffs clear.

Operators can useCISA’s guidance on prioritization and remediation⁠(opens in a new window)to assess how quickly to act based on exposure, exploitation, and potential impact. That may mean emergency patching, immediate mitigation, or a planned update, alongside forensic triage where warranted to assess whether systems have already been compromised. Priorities should be reassessed as conditions change, with a clear path to lasting remediation.

Global coordination depends on the people who maintain the software. Many projects are run by small teams that review security reports alongside routine development. Those teams need help separating new issues from duplicates, assessing impact, and testing fixes across supported releases. We support that work with funding, access to capable models, and hands-on engineering help.

Powerful AI capabilities are advancing across the industry, and we expect AI to play a growing role in helping defenders find vulnerabilities, monitor systems, and respond to threats. We’re investing in models, tools, and partnerships to help defenders put those capabilities to work.

Our investments include subscriptions for all maintainers throughCodex for OSSand direct sponsorship of projects such as theRust Foundation⁠(opens in a new window)for maintainers and technical work. Each project sets its own priorities. Reusable tests and security workflows can reduce the effort needed to handle future findings. Open-source projects canapply to Patch the Planet⁠(opens in a new window)for hands-on support.

We’re also calibrating additional blocking classifiers for Daybreak to help reduce the potential for misuse. This involves difficult tradeoffs: safeguards intended to prevent abuse can also block legitimate security work. Broad access to capable models and effective protections against misuse are both critical. Our aim is to preserve the capabilities defenders need to find and fix vulnerabilities while limiting harmful use. We’ll continue refining that balance as capabilities advance and we learn from how these tools are used.

As models become more capable, the opportunity extends beyond finding and fixing individual vulnerabilities. We want to help engineers build more secure software from the start. Improvements to a widely used component can prevent bugs or limit their impact across many products and services.

AI can help engineers understand existing code, prepare changes, and develop tests, while maintainers and security experts verify that those changes preserve the behavior users depend on. We see opportunities in several areas:

Secure code from the start.Coding models can help developers choose safer defaults, use security libraries correctly, and catch risky patterns as they write. Preventing vulnerabilities during development means fewer emergency fixes for maintainers and users.

Memory-safe software.Moving critical components to memory-safe languages can eliminate common classes of memory errors. AI can help with migrations, with tests and expert review to check behavior and compatibility.

articles.summary: OpenAI는 Calif가 GPT‑5.6 Sol을 활용해 PHP의 중대 취약점을 발견했으며, Wiz도 관련 취약점 두 건을 독립적으로 발견·보고했다고 밝혔다. PHP 유지관리자가 수정과 배포를 주도했고, 여러 보안 업체가 공개 전 보호 조치를 준비하는 데 참여했다. OpenAI는 취약할 가능성이 있는 PHP 버전을 식별하도록 돕는 Codex 스킬을 제공하며, 운영자는 유지관리자와 서비스 제공업체의 안내에 따라 업데이트를 적용해야 한다고 강조했다. 공격자보다 먼저 발견했다는 설명은 OpenAI가 파악한 범위의 판단이며, AI가 방어와 공격 양쪽의 속도를 높일 수 있다는 점이 핵심 시사점이다.

articles.title: Solving a 31-year-old grand challenge in mathematics – the KLS conjecture
articles.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension.  Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification.  For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab). They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab), established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase.  The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab), Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research.  Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged.  In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers.  Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements  Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project.  Opens in a new tabThe post Solving a 31-year-old grand challenge in mathematics – the KLS conjecture appeared first on Microsoft Research.
articles.summary: Microsoft Research는 연구진이 인간 주도 AI 연구 과정을 통해 31년간 미해결이던 KLS 추측을 해결했다고 발표했다. 이 결과는 로그오목 분포에서 평면 절단이 포착하는 병목과 최적의 임의 형태 절단 사이의 차이를 차원과 무관한 상수 배 이내로 제한하는 기하학적 원리를 다룬다. 연구자는 AI가 탐색한 수학적 가능성을 평가하고 가지치기하며 방향을 조정했고, 발표에 따르면 여러 독립 연구자의 검증과 기계 검증 형식화도 이뤄졌다. 고차원 확률·최적화·무작위 알고리즘의 이론적 기반에 중요한 결과지만, 제공된 자료에는 증명의 세부 내용이 포함되지 않았다.

articles.title: "AI 에이전트, 보안 판 바꾼다"…엔비디아 OpenShell 아키텍처 공개, 위험 행동 밀리초 만에 차단
articles.content:
엔비디아(NVIDIA)가 기업용 인공지능(AI) 에이전트의 실행 환경과 보안 통제 체계를 통합한 ‘엔비디아 오픈셸 레퍼런스 아키텍처(NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture)’를 공개했다. AI 에이전트가 기업 시스템과 외부 도구에 접근해 자율적으로 작업하는 환경에서 실행 권한을 관리하고, 이상 행동을 감시하며, 보안 정책 위반을 차단하는 인프라를 제공한다는 구상이다.

엔비디아는 21일(현지시간) 독일 베를린에서 열린 GTC에서 해당 아키텍처를 공개했다. 기업이 AI 에이전트를 개발하고 운영하는 데 필요한 컴퓨팅 인프라와 보안 소프트웨어를 결합해 대규모 에이전트 배포를 지원한다.

이번 아키텍처의 핵심은 AI 모델의 추론, 에이전트의 도구 사용, 보안 정책 집행을 각각 최적화된 컴퓨팅 구성 요소에 배치하는 것이다. 엔비디아는 이를 위해 베라 루빈(Vera Rubin) 인프라, 베라(Vera) CPU, 블루필드-4(BlueField-4) 데이터처리장치(DPU), 오픈소스 보안 런타임 소프트웨어인 오픈셸(OpenShell)을 결합했다.

젠슨 황(Jensen Huang) 엔비디아 창업자 겸 최고경영자(CEO)는 “AI 역량과 안전성은 함께 발전해야 한다”며 “기업이 수십억 개의 AI 에이전트 배포를 준비하는 상황에서 안전과 통제 기능은 컴퓨팅 아키텍처 자체에 내장돼야 한다”고 말했다.

베라 루빈·베라 CPU·블루필드-4로 역할 분담

아키텍처에서 베라 루빈은 AI 모델의 사전 학습과 사후 학습, 추론을 담당한다. 엔비디아는 에이전트 중심 워크로드에서 베라 루빈 NVL72 시스템이 메가와트당 처리량을 기존 대비 30배 높일 수 있다고 설명했다.

베라 CPU는 AI 에이전트의 실행 환경인 하네스(harness)와 도구 사용을 처리한다. 엔비디아는 베라 CPU가 x86 프로세서보다 2배 높은 성능과 향상된 에너지 효율을 제공한다고 밝혔다. 오픈셸은 이 환경에서 에이전트가 허용된 범위 안에서만 작업하도록 보안 경계를 설정한다.

보안 정책 집행은 블루필드-4 DPU와 엔비디아 센트리(NVIDIA Sentry)가 맡는다. 센트리는 엔비디아 도카(DOCA) 소프트웨어를 기반으로 에이전트의 행동을 지속적으로 감시하고, 소프트웨어 경계를 벗어나려는 행위를 하드웨어 수준에서 차단한다.

에이전트가 허용된 범위를 벗어나려 하면 센트리가 해당 에이전트를 격리하고 밀리초 단위로 실행을 중단할 수 있다는 것이 엔비디아의 설명이다. 엔비디아는 블루필드-4와 센트리의 결합으로 에이전트 처리 용량을 최대 20% 높일 수 있다고 덧붙였다.

이는 기존 보안 도구를 통해 사후에 이상 행위를 탐지하는 방식에서 나아가, 에이전트가 작업을 수행하는 동안 정책을 감시하고 위반 행위를 인프라 차원에서 집행하는 구조다. 특히 에이전트가 기업 데이터와 업무 시스템, 외부 도구에 접근하는 과정에서 권한 통제와 실행 격리를 강화하는 데 초점을 맞췄다.

클라우드부터 엣지까지...기업용 AI 생태계 확대

오픈셸 레퍼런스 아키텍처는 데이터센터뿐 아니라 엣지 환경에서도 활용할 수 있도록 설계됐다. 엔비디아 RTX 스파크(RTX Spark), DGX 스파크(DGX Spark), DGX 스테이션(DGX Station) 시스템을 통해 소매, 의료, 제조, 로봇, 소프트웨어 개발, 통신 등 다양한 산업의 에이전트 운영을 지원한다.

운영체제와 컨테이너 환경도 폭넓게 지원한다. 캐노니컬(Canonical), 수세(SUSE), 레드햇(Red Hat)의 리눅스 및 쿠버네티스 환경과 마이크로소프트 윈도우 기반 실행 환경인 마이크로소프트 이그제큐션 컨테이너(Microsoft Execution Containers)를 지원하며, 아마존웹서비스(AWS), 구글 클라우드(Google Cloud), 마이크로소프트 애저(Azure) 등 클라우드 환경에서도 사용할 수 있도록 했다.

AI 모델 공급업체로는 앤트로픽(Anthropic), 코히어(Cohere), 구글(Google), 메타(Meta), 오픈AI(OpenAI), 퍼플렉시티(Perplexity), 리플렉션(Reflection), 스페이스X 슈퍼 인텔리전스(SpaceX Super Intelligence) 등이 협력 대상에 포함됐다. 엔비디아는 이들과 함께 오픈셸 기반 에이전트 배포를 추진하고 있으며, 고도화된 모델 연구를 위한 적용도 협의하고 있다.

사이버보안 분야에서는 크라우드스트라이크(CrowdStrike), 시스코(Cisco), 체크포인트(Check Point), 포티넷(Fortinet), 팔로알토 네트웍스(Palo Alto Networks), 마이크로소프트, 옥타(Okta), 지스케일러(Zscaler) 등이 자사 에이전트 보안 솔루션에 대한 지원을 통합하고 있다. 델 테크놀로지스(Dell Technologies), HPE, 레노버(Lenovo), 슈퍼마이크로(Supermicro) 등 시스템 제조업체와 코어위브(CoreWeave), 오라클 클라우드 인프라스트럭처(Oracle Cloud Infrastructure) 등 클라우드 사업자도 관련 인프라 구축에 참여한다.

기업용 소프트웨어 분야에서는 SAP가 비즈니스 AI 플랫폼의 주울 스튜디오(Joule Studio) 런타임에 오픈셸 아키텍처를 통합하고 있다. 서비스나우(ServiceNow)는 장시간 실행되는 개인용 AI 에이전트 ‘서비스나우 아크(ServiceNow Arc)’를 일반에 공개하면서, 서비스나우의 슈퍼 인텔리전스 컨트롤 타워와 엔비디아 오픈셸을 통해 에이전트의 실행 권한과 정책을 통제하도록 했다. 회사는 AI 패스포트(AI Passport)를 통해 소프트웨어와 하드웨어 전반에서 에이전트 접근 권한을 수초 내에 철회할 수 있다고 밝혔다.

유럽의 BBVA와 산탄데르(Santander) 등 은행들도 오픈셸을 에이전트의 안전성·보안·거버넌스 강화를 위한 체계로 검토하고 있다. 다쏘시스템(Dassault Systèmes), IBM, 지멘스(Siemens), 시놉시스(Synopsys) 등 기업용 소프트웨어 업체도 관련 에이전트 플랫폼 개발에 참여한다.

엔비디아의 이번 발표는 AI 에이전트의 성능 향상뿐 아니라 기업 환경에서 자율 실행을 안전하게 관리할 수 있는 기반을 확보하려는 움직임으로 풀이된다. 에이전트가 복잡한 업무를 직접 수행하는 사례가 늘어날수록 접근 권한과 실행 범위를 명확히 정의하고, 정책 위반을 실시간으로 차단하는 기능이 중요해지기 때문이다.

다만 실제 도입 효과는 기업별 업무 환경과 보안 정책, 기존 시스템과의 통합 수준에 따라 달라질 수 있다. 오픈셸 레퍼런스 아키텍처의 확산 여부는 다양한 모델과 운영체제, 보안 제품을 아우르는 호환성과 함께 실제 운영 환경에서의 통제 효과에 달려 있을 것으로 보인다.

한편, 오픈셸 레퍼런스 아키텍처(다운)는 현재 이용할 수 있다. 상세 기술 문서는 엔비디아 공식 사이트(보기)에서 확인할 수 있다.(아래는 소개 영상)

articles.title: Mistral AI Releases Voxtral 3: Speech-to-Text, TTS and a Voice Agent SDK
articles.content: Mistral AI just released Voxtral 3. Mistral Voxtral 3 is a speech model family paired with a voice agent SDK. It ships 3 transcription models, 1 text-to-speech model and an SDK built on LiveKit. One place for listening, reasoning, tool calls and speaking. All 4 models are in public preview on the Mistral API. TL;DR Size: Voxtral Mini Transcribe 3 has 4B parameters. Small Transcribe 3 size: not disclosed. Both batch models list a 32k context. Runs on: Mistral API (EU, US and global endpoints) or your own infrastructure via Mistral sales. GPU and VRAM needs: not disclosed. Mistral says Mini suits resource-constrained environments. Performance: Top 3 on independent speech-to-text rankings, strongest on diarization and multilingual batch transcription. Best: 2.1% AA-WER for Small Transcribe 3, #3 on Artificial Analysis. Worst: Realtime at 240 ms: 7.4% WER on FLEURS 35, vs 4.2% for Gemini 3.5 Realtime. What is in the Voxtral 3 family? Mistral lists 4 models and 1 SDK: Voxtral Small Transcribe 3: flagship batch transcription and diarization. Docs also list translation, speech Q&A, summarization and function calling. Voxtral Mini Transcribe 3: a 4B model for cheaper, faster batch jobs. Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime 3: streaming ASR over WebSocket with end-of-turn detection. Voxtral Speech 3: text-to-speech, also called Voxtral Mini TTS 3 in the post. All transcription models support diarization and context biasing. Context biasing takes key terms or free text to improve recall. Batch transcription covers 50 languages, including 24 official EU languages. How does the Voxtral voice agent SDK work? The SDK is built on LiveKit and runs 3 stages as 1 streaming pipeline. Realtime Transcribe 3 listens and detects when the caller stops speaking. A general LLM, such as Mistral Small 4, reasons and calls tools. Voxtral Speech 3 replies in the tone of the conversation so far. Each turn completes in under 1 second. The agent stops talking when the caller cuts in. It handles phone calls over SIP and browser or app sessions over WebRTC. Because each stage is a separate model, teams can swap the LLM, voice or language. && How accurate is Voxtral Transcribe 3? These numbers are self-reported by Mistral: FLEURS 45 (WER, forced / inferred language): Small 4.1% / 4.0%. MAI-Transcribe-2 ties at 4.1% / 4.0%. Mini 4.6% / 4.5%. Whisper large-v3 16.0% / 14.9%. Diarization (cpWER, 5 public sets): Small 18.4% and Mini 18.6%. Pyannote scores 19.0% and MAI-Transcribe-2 20.3%. Keyphrase recall (Earnings 22): Small 94.6% with context, 81.4% without. Scribe v2 posts 94.3% and 84.0%. On Artificial Analysis, Small scores 2.1% AA-WER and Mini 2.2%. Only Fun-Realtime-ASR-preview (1.7%) and MAI-Transcribe-2 (2.0%) rank higher. Speed is the gap: Small’s speed factor is 65.8x, against 307.5x for MAI-Transcribe-2. How do realtime transcription and TTS compare? On FLEURS 35, the realtime model trades latency for accuracy. It scores 5.7% WER at 2,400 ms and 6.4% at 480 ms. At 240 ms, WER rises to 7.4%. Gemini 3.5 Realtime Transcribe scores 4.2% and MAI-Transcribe-2 Streaming 5.8%. GPT Live Transcribe (8.4%) and Scribe v2 Realtime (8.7%) trail every Voxtral setting. Voxtral Speech 3 costs $13 per 1M characters. Mistral says that undercuts OpenAI TTS-1, Deepgram, ElevenLabs Flash and Gemini Flash. Explicit controls cover emotion, pacing and emphasis. The model page lists ~90 ms time-to-first-audio and 34 emotion tags. Pro Voice adapts a speaker’s style from 30 minutes of audio. Artificial Analysis places it in the top 12 of both TTS arenas. Per Mistral’s price table: Voxtral Mini Transcribe 3 (batch): $0.0035/min Voxtral Small Transcribe 3: $0.004/min Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime 3: $0.008/min Voxtral Speech 3 (batch and realtime): $13 per 1M characters Voice agent API: $0.04/min with Mistral Small 4, $0.08/min with any other reasoning model The models run on Mistral’s European, US and global endpoints. OpenRouter also lists all 3 new models with EU-hosted, zero-data-retention endpoints. Key Takeaways Voxtral 3 bundles 3 ASR models, 1 TTS model and a LiveKit voice agent SDK. Small Transcribe 3 hits 2.1% AA-WER, #3 on Artificial Analysis. Best-in-chart diarization: 18.4% cpWER, ahead of Pyannote and MAI-Transcribe-2. Batch transcription costs $0.0035 to $0.004 per minute; TTS costs $13 per 1M characters. Realtime accuracy trails Gemini 3.5 Realtime, and no open weights were announced. articles.title: Recursive Releases Flint, an Open-Weight 40B MoE Local Coding Model for Agents with 2.5B Active Params
articles.content: Recursive Superintelligence has released Flint, its first model. The Recursive Flint local coding model is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 40B total and 2.5B active parameters. Recursive team states that its Eureka Machine, an automated research system, helped build nearly every part of the stack. The weights are on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. TL;DR Size: 39.8B total, about 2.5B active per token. Context: 262,144 tokens documented on the model card; the blog cites up to 512k. Runs on: 48 GB Apple Silicon Macs (M4 Pro, M5 Pro, M5 Max) or 48 GB NVIDIA GPUs. 4-bit weights take about 23 GB. Performance: Tops Recursive’s chart among MoE models under 50B on agentic coding. Trails the strongest dense models. Best: IFEval 95.1%. SWE-bench Verified 74.2%. Worst: Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 54.9%, versus 73.0% for dense Qwen 3.8. What is Recursive Flint? Flint is a decoder-only MoE Transformer for coding agents. The model investigates codebases, fixes bugs, implements features and writes tests. It is text-only and supports reasoning and OpenAI-compatible tool calls. Introducing Flint, @Recursive_SI’s first model: a fast local coding model built with our automated research system, the Eureka Machine.• Best-in-class fast local coding• Up to 2x faster than comparable models: 125+ tokens/sec on a MacBook Pro, 150+ on RTX Spark• Built from… pic.twitter.com/ufg2xScSGw— Richard Socher (@RichardSocher) October 21, 2026 How does Flint’s architecture work? Flint has 49 layers: 2 dense layers, then 47 MoE layers. Each MoE layer has 256 routed experts. A router selects 6 per token, plus 1 always-active shared expert. Attention mixes 2 types. 35 layers use a 513-token sliding window. 14 layers use full attention with no positional encoding. There are 32 query heads and 4 key/value heads. The 2.5B active figure includes the output head. The active body alone is about 2.2B parameters. How did the Eureka Machine build Flint? The Eureka Machine proposes ideas, implements them, tests them and picks what to try next. Recursive highlights 3 contributions: Architecture: It started from a 35B-total, 3B-active baseline. It searched expert configurations and widths, landing on 40B total and 2.5B active. Quantization: It quantized the output layer (lm_head) to 4 bits, against common practice. An offline distillation stage, with the 16-bit model as teacher, recovered accuracy. This nearly halved training steps versus a quantization-aware training baseline. The NVFP4 model scores within 0.7 points of the 16-bit model. Kernels: It wrote specialized kernels for low-bit projections, MoE operations, attention and prompt processing. On M4 and M5 chips, a Metal megakernel fuses the entire decode forward pass. How does Flint perform on coding benchmarks? All scores below are self-reported by Recursive. Sampling used temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95 and top-k 20. Solutions found through web retrieval counted as failures. SWE-bench runs used mini-swe-agent with no internet access. Agentic scores average pass@1 over at least 5 attempts. In Recursive’s chart, Qwen3.6 scores 73.4% on SWE-bench Verified. Dense Qwen 3.8 scores 73.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, well above Flint. Recursive reports more than 125 tokens per second on an M4 Pro MacBook Pro. It reports more than 150 tokens per second on a 64 GB NVIDIA RTX Spark. Both are short-context figures, up to 2x faster than comparable models. It also claims Flint runs more than 5x faster than dense 25-40B models with similar coding scores. There are 3 local options: Apple Silicon: Flint INT4 MLX weights take about 22.6 GB. The rec engine needs an M4 Pro, M5 Pro or M5 Max with 48 GB memory. It reports 1.4 to 2.6x the throughput of llama.cpp on an M4 Pro. NVIDIA: The NVFP4 GGUF file is 22.9 GB. Recursive recommends at least 48 GB of GPU memory. Server: The 80 GB BF16 checkpoint needs 1 B300 or H200 GPU per replica. Flint also works with llama.cpp, Ollama, Unsloth, LM Studio, vLLM and SGLang. Key Takeaways Flint is a 40B MoE coding model with only 2.5B active parameters. It scores 74.2% on SWE-bench Verified and 54.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. 4-bit weights run in about 23 GB on a 48 GB Mac or GPU. Recursive’s Eureka Machine helped design the architecture, quantization and kernels. SWE-bench Pro v2 scores are Recursive-measured and not comparable to public SWE-Bench Pro. articles.title: Google Open-Sources TorchTPU, a Native PyTorch Backend for Cloud TPUs
articles.content: Google has open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend for Cloud TPUs. It was co-developed with the PyTorch team at Meta and announced at PyTorch Conference 2026 on October 20, 2026. Existing PyTorch code targets a TPU through a standard torch.device("tpu"). TPUs now sit beside GPUs and CPUs as a native PyTorch device. Google team states that TorchTPU replaces PyTorch/XLA and recommends it for all new workloads. TL;DR Size: A software stack, not a model. 4 open repos: TorchTPU, vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, TorchTitan. TorchTPU is v0.2.0 on PyPI, Python 3.11+, Apache 2.0. Runs on: Google Cloud TPUs. Tested on generations from v5e, scaled to 8,192 Ironwood (TPU7x) chips. Serving supports FP8, MXFP4 and NVFP4 checkpoints. Performance: Eager mode for debugging, torch.compile for production-level throughput. Best: 52% MFU training Qwen 3 8B with TorchTitan on Ironwood (self-reported). Worst: Out-of-box eager took 11.49s per step in a fine-tuning case, versus 2.78s fully tuned. What is TorchTPU? TorchTPU is an open-source PyTorch backend from Google and Meta that runs PyTorch models natively on TPUs. It plugs in through PyTorch’s PrivateUse1 interface. Tensors are ordinary PyTorch tensors, with no subclasses or wrappers. It runs one process per device and preserves tensor views and in-place mutations. The predecessor, PyTorch/XLA, recorded lazy-tensor graphs. Developers often added code to mark compilable regions. PyTorch/XLA also only supported pure SPMD code. TorchTPU also handles divergent MPMD execution. How does TorchTPU execute PyTorch code? TorchTPU ships 3 eager modes: Strict (default): dispatches each operator asynchronously with standard PyTorch semantics. Debug: runs synchronously with tensor bounds checking. DeferAndFuse: fuses runs of eager operators to cut HBM traffic. The TorchTPU paper says it can be 50% or more faster than Strict. For peak speed, torch.compile(backend="tpu") captures the graph with TorchDynamo. It lowers through StableHLO to OpenXLA, which emits TPU machine code. Compiled executables are cached across processes, hosts and job restarts. Custom Pallas kernels are callable as standard PyTorch functions. Prebuilt Tokamax kernels and Helion tile kernels also work. Distribution uses the tpu_dist process group. It supports DDP, FSDP2 and DTensor, along with a topology-aware mesh for TPU interconnects. How fast is TorchTPU? All figures below are self-reported by Google and partners. Training scale: TorchTitan reached up to 52% MFU on Qwen 3 8B. Google reports near-linear scaling up to 8,192 Ironwood TPUs. Tuning ladder: In a TorchTitan fine-tuning case, step time fell from 11.49s to 2.78s. DeferAndFuse alone gave 1.15x. Full torch.compile gave 3.80x. Model coverage: Google continuously tests about 5,000 Hugging Face models in eager and compiled modes. Fleet serving: Zenteiq grew daily output from 1.47B to 5.97B tokens per 1,000 TPU v6e chips. That gain came from llm-d routing on GKE, not TorchTPU alone. && What integrations ship with TorchTPU? Hugging Face: Transformers v5 deploys to TPU with device_map="tpu". Diffusers supports eager, torch.compile and tensor parallelism. vLLM-TorchTPU: built with Inferact. Keeps upstream schedulers and API servers, with custom Pallas kernels. SGLang-TorchTPU: built with RadixArk. Keeps RadixAttention prefix reuse. Serving features: FP8 KV caches, FP8, MXFP4 and NVFP4 checkpoints. Speculative decoding includes MTP and EAGLE-3. TorchTitan: recipes for Llama 3 70B/405B, Qwen 3 8B/32B, Qwen 3 235B MoE and FLUX.1 12B. Also: llm-d 1.0, Ray, TorchRec, VeRL (preview) and LiteRT-Torch for on-device export. How does TorchTPU compare with PyTorch/XLA, TorchNeuron and JAX? articles.title: Google Cloud Ships llm-d 1.0 With Cache-Aware Routing for TPU and GPU Fleets
articles.content: Google team have released llm-d 1.0, the first stable version of its distributed inference stack. This open-source, Kubernetes-native layer turns vLLM or SGLang model servers into one coordinated pool. They released it at the PyTorch Conference North America. It targets self-hosted agent and RL workloads, where round-robin load balancing breaks down. TL;DR A serving stack: Google reports a published benchmark on a 17,000-node multi-region GKE deployment. Runs on: Kubernetes with NVIDIA, AMD or Intel GPUs or Google TPUs, over vLLM or SGLang. Performance: Vendor-reported gains come from cache-aware routing, tiered KV cache offload and prefill/decode disaggregation. Best: Median TTFT cut by more than 85%, with 2.4x throughput, on an Ironwood TPU coding workload. Worst: RL time-slicing lifts accelerator duty cycle only to above 70%, so roughly 30% idle time remains. What is llm-d 1.0? llm-d was founded in 2025 by Red Hat, IBM, Google Cloud, CoreWeave and NVIDIA. Red Hat, IBM and Google are the lead maintainers. The project counts more than 500 contributors from over 25 organizations. It is a CNCF Sandbox project, accepted on March 12, 2026, and is licensed under Apache 2.0. Prefix-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch inference already shipped. Version 1.0 is about running them reliably in production, which IBM calls day 2 operations. What is new in llm-d 1.0? Multi-tenant quality of service: Priority and fairness-aware flow control stops bursty agents from starving latency-sensitive requests. Stable foundation: v1 APIs and a hardened request path, validated on multiple clouds and accelerators. Zero-downtime upgrades: Router high availability with hot standby, plus DisaggregatedSet, which rolls prefill and decode pools together. Agent-aware serving: Session-aware routing, turn-priority scheduling and native Responses API state. Async inference: llm-d-async-processor pulls jobs from Google Cloud Pub/Sub or Redis into slack capacity. Expanded TPU support: TorchTPU runs PyTorch models natively inside upstream vLLM and SGLang. How does llm-d route requests? The llm-d router builds on the Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extension. It tracks which replicas hold each cached prefix. It then weighs load and predicted latency before picking a replica. Agents call one endpoint, and each step lands where its context already lives. When accelerator memory fills, KV cache moves to host memory, then SSD or Managed Lustre. It uses vLLM’s OffloadingConnector, Mooncake or SGLang’s HiCache for this. How OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research used distributed AI agents to help scientists identify promising research leads in data from millions of brain cells

See how OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research deployed thousands of AI agents in parallel to identify promising biological connections in complex data from millions of brain cells.

⁠

Video credit: PerturbAI.

What if scientists could uncover new clues about Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s in minutes instead of months? Working together, OpenAI,PerturbAI⁠(opens in a new window), andScripps Research⁠(opens in a new window)usedthousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind⁠(opens in a new window)to analyze and interpret existing experimental data frommillions of mouse brain cells⁠(opens in a new window)in just 32 minutes. The agents connected the effects of gene disruptions with findings from scientific literature, uncovering unexpected biological connections that can help scientists understand disease and identify research directions for new treatments. The work shows how AI can help researchers explore more of what large biological experiments reveal.

Modern experiments generate far more data than scientists can thoroughly investigate. Researchers can now alter thousands of genes and measure their effects across millions of cells. But understanding what these results mean for human disease requires connecting complex experimental findings with decades of scattered scientific knowledge. This is where AI can help scientists uncover promising leads that might otherwise be missed.

The team divided the analysis among thousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind, an approach we call distributed biological reasoning. The agents examined awhole-brain CRISPR atlas⁠(opens in a new window), a dataset showing how gene disruptions affect different types of cells across the mouse brain. Each agent investigated a gene disruption, analyzed cellular responses, searched scientific literature, and proposed explanations for the results. Their reports were combined into a reasoning atlas linking genes, cellular effects, relevant publications, and possible biological mechanisms.

The research team estimated that comparable human analysis and literature review, conducted one perturbation at a time, would take months to a year. The agents reproduced findings from human analyses while uncovering additional leads. Their assessments of novelty and scientific value also aligned with judgments from blinded human experts. These findings help prioritize further experiments needed to test the proposed biological mechanisms.

Some of these insights point to new leads for understanding brain disease. The agents identified unexpected differences in how two disease-linked genes affect brain cells differently, as well as a potential connection between cholesterol regulation and neurodegeneration. These findings could help scientists investigate how disease develops and where future treatments might intervene.

Researchers can begin exploring these findings today. The reasoning atlas isavailable⁠(opens in a new window), allowing scientists to compare related genes, investigate unexpected responses, and identify promising leads to pursue. New discoveries often emerge when researchers from different fields bring their expertise together and connect familiar ideas in unexpected ways. AI can significantly scale these connections by linking new data with knowledge scattered across disciplines. The opportunity goes beyond analyzing data faster. By combining AI with experimental biology, human expertise, and scientific literature, we can help scientists turn more of their data into testable ideas.

Some of an experiment’s most interesting clues lie outside the story scientists set out to investigate. In a dataset spanning thousands of perturbations, those clues can be easy to miss.

The agents identified an unexpected difference between Tsc1 and Tsc2, two genes that work together to control mTOR, a major regulator of cell growth, metabolism, and aging. Disrupting either gene had similar effects in several groups of neurons. But in the cerebellum, which helps coordinate movement, Tsc2 disruption altered the activity of dozens of genes involved in neuronal communication, while Tsc1 disruption produced little change.

That difference may be relevant to human disease. In people with tuberous sclerosis, abnormalities in the cerebellum are strongly linked to TSC2 mutations. While medicines that reduce mTOR activity can treat certain brain tumors and seizures, learning and behavioral difficulties associated with the disease remain challenging to address. The agents pinpointed a specific group of neurons and cellular changes worth investigating: which changes might existing medicines correct, and which might point to new treatment approaches? This gives researchers a more specific set of questions to test in the lab.

Could a single agent given the entire dataset do just as well as thousands of agents working in parallel? We tested this while keeping the model and resources fixed. As the workload grew, the single agent searched less of the literature, citing only 11 references at the largest workload, while the distributed agents cited more than 700 references. Human experts also preferred the distributed-agent interpretations.

Scientists have limited time and often focus on the strongest signals in their data. Distributed agents can help examine a wider range of responses, including subtle or unexpected ones, and connect them with relevant scientific literature. Running the agents in parallel allows many perturbations to be investigated at once. This helps scientists explore more of what an experiment contains and identify promising leads that might otherwise be missed.

At the largest workload, distributed agents cited more than 700 references, compared with 11 for a single agent.

A finding becomes more valuable when it points to an experiment worth doing. The agents found one such lead inDCTN1, a gene whose mutations cause Perry syndrome, a neurodegenerative disease with Parkinson-like symptoms.

DCTN1 is involved in moving cargo inside neurons. In the whole-brain CRISPR atlas, disrupting Dctn1 increased the expression of genes involved in making cholesterol. The agents connected this observation with research suggesting that problems with cholesterol transport may cause cells to make more cholesterol. This raised a question for follow-up experiments: could DCTN1 disruption change how cholesterol is distributed within neurons, and could those changes contribute to neurodegeneration? If so, could restoring normal cholesterol distribution help protect neurons?

Human experts also considered this hypothesis novel, consequential and worth following up on. This example shows how connecting an unexpected result with existing knowledge can turn a clue into a testable idea, and potentially a new direction for treating disease.

In blinded comparisons, human experts preferred distributed-agent reports over single-agent reports 75% of the time.

Scientists remain at the center of discovery. By uncovering more promising leads, AI can help researchers decide which ideas to pursue, design experiments, and interpret results. The goal is to turn more of the information in biological experiments into knowledge that, over time, can help guide the development of better medicines.

October 21, 2026

Over the past few months, we’ve worked with customers and partners to align safety policies across services that provide our models. We’re also updating our Usage Policies to make those requirements clearer and easier for developers to follow.

Models such as GPT‑6 Astra expand what developers and businesses can build. As those capabilities grow, we’re working to keep safeguards effective and consistently applied across the services that offer our models.

Before deploying a model, we evaluate its capabilities and risks, train it to follow safety requirements, and test whether its safeguards hold up when people deliberately try to bypass them. As we describe in ourapproach to safety and alignment, we combine safeguards designed to reinforce one another.

After deployment, we monitor for potential abuse and investigate concerns. Tomitigate cyber misuse, for example, we train models to refuse harmful requests and use systems that look for suspicious patterns across interactions to decide how to respond. Trusted access programs provide another layer of protection and set eligibility requirements and conditions for access to our most powerful capabilities.

Some safeguards are built into the model and others depend on the systems and people around it. Both need to be effective whether people access our models directly or through a partner.

Developers and businesses should be able to choose where they access our models, with consistent safeguards across those services. We developed policies to align our safeguards across providers and are working with each of our partners to ensure their implementation meets or exceeds our safety standards. These policies apply whether people access our models directly through OpenAI, partners that host them, or through reseller partners.

These policies require partners that provide access to OpenAI models to maintain safeguards consistent with our own, investigate potential violations, and take appropriate action when concerns are identified. That includes coordinating on enforcement so that restrictions remain effective across services providing access to our models.

Putting this into practice means accounting for how different services work and how customers use them. Our work with customers and partners onPrivate Safety Processingis one example of how we can develop effective safeguards while giving customers greater choice and control over their sensitive data.

We’re also updating ourUsage Policies, effective November 20, 2026, to clarify the rules for safe model development and sensitive uses of AI. The updated Usage Policies build on that work by requiring services that provide direct access to our models such as model routers or AI gateways to get our review and approval before offering that access.

We’ll keep explaining what’s allowed, what’s restricted, and how customers and partners can ask questions or resolve compliance concerns.

As our models become more capable, we’ll keep improving how we detect, investigate, and respond to misuse. Customers can face misuse through their end users, compromised accounts, or leaked API keys and we work with them to understand and address those problems.

We’re also working with customers to introduce SafetyIDs, which customers can provide to help us distinguish between individual end users in an investigation without OpenAI learning those users’ identities. With SafetyIDs, we can respond to potential misuse more precisely while reducing disruption to others.

We base enforcement decisions on documented conduct and risk, apply our rules consistently, and respond in proportion to the circumstances. When we restrict access, we revisit those restrictions if meaningful changes in conduct, commitments, or safeguards address the concerns behind our decision.

We want more people to benefit from AI. Clear rules and consistent safeguards should make it easier for developers and businesses to build, compete, and choose the services that work best for them.

By Ritendra Datta and Karthik Gopalratnam, Members of Technical Staff

Traditional advertising systems are built to respond to discrete units of user intent. A user searches for or views something online, the ads system receives those queries and page views as events, and the system looks for matching ads based on those events.  Building an ads stack for ChatGPT was different: user intent develops across conversations and shifts over multiple turns of a conversation, sometimes without a fitting advertising moment. To support this new paradigm, we built a bespoke ads delivery system. This new type of ad stack is based on a custom, post-trained frontier LLM that makes tool calls for retrieval (identifying the top options), ranking (predicting user engagement), relevance (evaluating the usefulness of the ad), and running auctions for final ad selection and pricing.

Our ads system supports the nuance of evolving user goals by making three key design decisions: 1) implementing stateful ads sessions, meaning information is remembered across turns of a conversation and across multiple conversations, 2) relying on a custom, post-trained LLM that uses a tool call architecture to interpret a conversation’s context and underlying intent, and then effectively select, rank, and deliver ads, and 3) running the ads selection process separately from ChatGPT’s answer generation, in its own service, to keep ads from influencing answers and maintain ChatGPT’s neutral voice. We use our post-trained LLM to orchestrate the entire ads flow, determining the right ad to surface at the right time based on both the user’s current turn and conversation history. While bootstrapping a self-improving ads system like this used to take years, ChatGPT Ads reached $1 billion in annualized revenue run rateless than 200 days after launch; now, more than 100,000 advertisers have run ads on ChatGPT since launch.

A conventional advertising request usually starts with a well-defined event. A user submits a search query or opens a webpage and the ads system receives a request. This type of system is fairly simple: it retrieves potential ad candidates, ranks them, runs an auction to appropriately price the opportunity, and shows the resulting ad to the user. ChatGPT does not naturally produce such a concrete moment.

In a ChatGPT conversation, people arrive with goals rather than a one-answer search query. They might be planning a trip, choosing software for their business, furnishing a home, or learning a new hobby. This doesn’t all happen in one turn of a conversation. ChatGPT often helps the user clarify what matters along the way.

As an example, our engineering team asked ChatGPT how to train for a race: A conversation begins with a general question about running. Several turns later, they ask about shoes to help train. The commercial meaning of the conversation changes as each constraint arrives—and this personalized context evolves across multiple sessions. A system that acted on the first message could retrieve the wrong intent entirely, potentially degrading the user’s experience and getting in their way.

Building our ads system required us to move beyond the request-response advertising architecture and build an ads stack from scratch to find potential economic opportunities while prioritizing user trust and value.

Turning every message into a standalone request, like a traditional ads system, would have carried a few risks in our chat use case: 1) misreading the user goal by oversimplifying it, 2) beginning the advertising flow too soon, before the user’s real need has become clear, 3) showing ads that get in the way of the user journey instead of supporting it, and 4) inefficiently rerunning the ads flow every time the request changes, creating noise and wasting cost. Instead of building around individual events, the ads system (consisting of retrieval, ranking, and delivery) maintains a stateful session, meaning the ads session runs for the duration of an eligible turn, remembering and updating information as it evolves. ChatGPT sends the initial request context to the ads server. The ads system follows and adapts to the developing exchange rather than relying on a single flattened query.

The ads selection process runs alongside ChatGPT’s normal response generation to ensure the ads flow doesn’t influence ChatGPT’s responses. Ads are filtered and selected through a separate system consuming the conversation under its own eligibility, quality, and delivery constraints. This important architectural boundary—different services that use separate models and separate code—lets core ChatGPT servers handle generating the organic response; meanwhile,  the ads system independently evaluates whether there’s an appropriate advertising opportunity and, if so, prepares a sponsored placement through a separate serving process.

Advertising runs alongside the ChatGPT answer path.

Beyond protecting the user experience, this separation has some practical consequences. ChatGPT has no dependency on the ads system—the services are in no way intertwined and don’t share a content generation model. So if the ads serving system is unavailable or slow, ChatGPT’s organic response continues unaffected. This means the ads system can’t take down or delay the ChatGPT product. The other benefit of this separation is that it keeps the bar very high for valuable ads. Returning no ad is an ordinary, successful outcome. The system only delivers an ad if it’s clearly beneficial to users and advertisers.

The other key architectural component in our ads stack is the post-trained LLM that interprets conversations and runs the entire ads flow in an agentic loop—making tool calls to the core functions of the ads system, from the retrieval stage to ranking to auction and, ultimately, delivery. We call this LLM theorchestrator.

The first part of an ads flow is understanding user intent to start the retrieval process, which is a fast and deliberately broad sourcing of potential ads to later filter through. Receiving the conversation incrementally creates a richer but more ambiguous retrieval problem because the ads system needs to distinguish current intent from stale context. The orchestrator must interpret references to earlier messages, recognize when a user is speaking hypothetically, and avoid treating every mention of a product or service as a request to buy something.

The ads orchestrator uses the available conversation and user context, iterating to find good ads and repeatedly choosing when to call which tool with the underlying goal of finding the most appropriate ad (the ad that balances high user value and high advertiser value) for that conversation and context. If the user chooses to personalize ads, the orchestrator also considers available nonsensitive information about the user’s past conversations to find the best ad matches.

The ads orchestrator iteratively calls ads delivery tools to find valuable ads.

As the conversation progresses and the ads orchestrator gets more updated information, the orchestrator can run a fresh set of tool calls with the updated context to find better ads and return them to the client, which can then use these new ads if they arrive in time.

Printed Throw Pillow

The orchestrator is designed to balance user value and advertiser value, always putting users first.

The ads system consists of individual tools, and the orchestrator calls them iteratively to find the best ads for a conversation. At a high level, the orchestrator turns conversations into brief text summaries, which are then turned into semantic embeddings (stored meanings that are easier for an ads system to sift through), retrieves ad candidates using those semantic embeddings, filters those candidates for eligibility (based on budget, user settings, and other preliminary checks), assesses their quality and relevance, and does a final ranking to identify high value opportunities for placement at the end of a chat response. Each ad must therefore meet a high bar on eligibility and relevance in order to be eligible for placement.

The orchestrator LLM first prepares one or more queries representing the relevant commercial intent. This can include rewriting conversation context to broaden the commercial possibilities beyond 1:1 search queries and then creating semantic representations, where the orchestrator distills a multiturn conversation into a summarized version for the retrieval system—retrieving ads from our database in a focused way.

Ad placements will be better for both users and advertisers if they only appear when there’s deep understanding of the user’s intent. Multiple queries can preserve different aspects of intent. A conversation about planning a trip, for example, might contain distinct needs related to transportation, lodging, or activities. The retrieval system can preserve these distinctions rather than compressing the entire conversation into one literal string.

As an example, let’s look at a potential conversation sequence about hiking shoes:

What should I cover on a two-day trip to Yosemite?

Will it be cold next week?

New [insert brand] product lines?

Although the user hasn’t connected the shoe brand question to the Yosemite trip, this conversation might be represented in our ads system by two queries, such as[shoes appropriate for hiking trip]and[new [brand] product lines good for travel]. This might only be the first attempt; the orchestrator is designed to iterate on these representations until it finds ads in our inventory that are highly valuable to the user.

Retrieval is the process of creating a deliberately broad pool of ad options. Candidates may come from different retrieval strategies and can later compete under the same serving constraints. articles.title: Vercel Open-Sources durable-harness for Crash-Proof Coding Agents
articles.content: Vercel has released durable-harness, an open-source package that keeps coding agent sessions alive through crashes and timeouts. Vercel durable-harness wraps existing harnesses, including Pi, OpenCode, Claude Code and Codex, without changing them. Each session lives in a durable log. A dead function no longer means lost work. For teams moving agents off laptops and into the cloud, that closes a real gap. TL;DR Size: npm package, version 0.0.x, Apache-2.0. Adapters cover 5 harnesses: Pi, OpenCode, fx, Claude Code, Codex. Runs on: Vercel Functions plus Vercel Queues, Node.js 22+ with Postgres, or laptop files. Claude Code and Codex need a Vercel Sandbox. Performance: No latency or throughput benchmarks published. All recovery claims are self-reported by Vercel. Best: Finished model and tool calls are read back from the log, never re-run or billed twice. Worst: Experimental 0.0.x API. Claude Code and Codex run only in a Vercel Sandbox, even self-hosted. What is durable-harness? durable-harness is a set of adapters from Vercel that store a harness session in a Workflow SDK World. A World bundles storage, a queue and a stream behind one interface. The package uses the same machinery that powers Vercel’s Workflow SDK. Why do coding agents lose work in the cloud? Harnesses like Pi and Claude Code were designed as long-lived local processes. They keep the session in memory. Locally, the workspace and history sit on the same disk, so resuming takes 1 prompt. In the cloud, a VM with persistent storage does not track which calls completed. Vercel team notes a failed turn or network error then means lost work. How does durable-harness work? It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model or tool call runs, it records an intent. When the call finishes, it records the outcome. Each turn is backed by a message on Vercel Queues. If the function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function. That function reads the log and continues. After a crash, the log shows what finished, what was running and what never started: Completed calls are read from the log, so finished model tokens are not billed again. replay: 'safe' tools, such as lookups, can run again. replay: 'never' tools, such as refunds, never run twice. The model is told the call may have happened. Harness session files are mirrored into the log as well. That covers Claude Code’s transcript, Codex’s rollout and OpenCode’s event store. Where do files and shell commands run? Model-chosen commands never run on the function’s own disk. The tools docs list 3 workspace options: virtual() keeps files in the session log, with a bash-compatible shell and no network. It holds about 500 files. virtual({ durable: false }) keeps scratch files in memory and clears them every turn. sandbox() gives each session a Vercel Sandbox, with /workspace on a Drive. Typed JSON documents, such as a to-do list, also live in the log. Each holds at most 64 KB. articles.title: A general-purpose System One decision model for clinical records
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.27099v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical care, health-system operations and biomedical discovery depend on extracting reliable answers from patient records, yet applying diverse clinical questions across entire populations remains computationally expensive. Here we present Clinical System One (CS1), a 4-billion-parameter decision model for fast, typed judgments from clinical records, along with two agentic harnesses in which CS1 works together with a generalist language model. CS1-4B is trained on 12.4 million questions and answers from 3.6 million patients across a multi-hospital health system, combining structured-data keys, observed outcomes and language-model supervision across clinical notes, diagnostic reports and patient timelines. It answers multiple typed questions in a single forward pass without task-specific retraining, and each answer carries a probability that can route uncertain cases to human review. On 963,408 held-out patients, CS1-4B outperformed open decision models up to 27 billion parameters on 13 of 14 tasks scored independently of its training teacher. Across 21 external data sets, its aggregate performance approached that of the strongest tested 27-billion-parameter model, with 6.4-fold faster inference in a matched workload. Integrating CS1-4B with a language model agent produced cited answers over complete multi-year patient histories and screened a patient population against the eligibility criteria of 17 registered clinical trials, placing four times as many judged-eligible patients among its top 20 candidates as keyword search while using 690-fold fewer language-model tokens than a language model reading every record. These findings support a division of labour in clinical AI, with small decision models performing repeated record reading and generative models formulating questions and synthesizing evidence.
articles.summary: Clinical System One은 임상 기록에서 여러 유형의 질문에 한 번의 순전파로 답하고 각 답변의 확률을 제공하는 40억 파라미터 판단 모델이다. 연구진은 360만 환자의 1,240만 질문·답변으로 학습했으며, 별도 평가 환자 약 96만 명에서 교사 모델과 독립적으로 채점한 14개 과제 중 13개에서 최대 270억 파라미터의 공개 판단 모델보다 좋은 결과를 보고했다. 21개 외부 데이터셋에서는 가장 강력한 비교 대상 270억 모델에 근접한 종합 성능과 동일 조건 작업에서 6.4배 빠른 추론을 보였다. 작은 모델이 반복적인 기록 판독을 맡고 생성형 에이전트가 질문과 근거 종합을 담당하는 분업을 제안하지만, 실제 임상 도입 효과를 확정한 결과는 아니다.

articles.title: SceneRig: An Agentic System for Simulation-Ready 3D Scene Reconstruction from Single Images
articles.content: Simulation is a powerful tool for robotics, but building diverse, simulation-ready scenes at scale remains difficult. Reconstructing scenes from single images is a promising alternative, but visual similarity alone is insufficient: objects must also be recovered, accurately placed, and physically grounded. Existing methods that rely on post-hoc physics settling often misplace objects, producing scenes that look correct but behave poorly under manipulation. We present SceneRig, an agentic system that turns a single image into an editable, simulation-ready scene. SceneRig combines geometric, visual, and physical tools to reconstruct a faithful 3D scene. An agent then performs edit-and-validate loops inside a physics simulator to achieve physical stability. Across diverse inputs, SceneRig improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement while keeping the reconstructed scenes physically stable. Furthermore, SceneRig is effective for downstream robotics: its scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline method and more reliably support replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.
articles.summary: SceneRig는 단일 이미지에서 편집 가능하고 물리 시뮬레이션에 사용할 수 있는 3D 장면을 만드는 에이전트 시스템이다. 기하·시각·물리 도구로 객체와 배치를 복원한 뒤, 시뮬레이터 안에서 수정과 검증을 반복해 물리적 안정성을 확보한다. 연구진은 객체 분할·외형·배치 개선뿐 아니라 실제 로봇 정책의 결과 예측과 기록된 조작 동작 재현에서도 비교 방법보다 나은 결과를 보고했다. 단순히 비슷하게 보이는 3D 복원을 넘어 로봇 학습과 평가에 사용할 수 있는 장면을 생성하는 데 의의가 있다.

articles.title: PROVISO: Provenance-Informed Action Selection for Secure LLM Agents
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.27115v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents act on the external world through tools and third-party skills, so a single executed action can cause irreversible harm. Existing defenses judge a proposed action without tracking whether its content comes from the user or from external sources such as tool outputs, and they judge it in isolation rather than against an available alternative, which forces a trade-off between security and utility. We present PROVISO, a controller that decides which action to commit after the agent proposes an action and before it is executed. PROVISO encodes trusted observations, external observations, the proposed action, and an alternative into provenance-typed memory, relates them through role-specific queries, and commits the action with the highest calibrated value learned from outcomes. On four agent security tasks spanning the agent lifecycle, no baseline exceeds PROVISO in both security and utility. PROVISO improves F1 over the strongest baseline by 13.84 points on SkillsBench and by 7.07 points on ToolSafe, and it reaches 88-99 F1 on three additional skill detection benchmarks.
articles.summary: PROVISO는 LLM 에이전트가 도구를 실행하기 직전에 제안된 행동과 대안을 비교해 실행 여부를 결정하는 보안 제어기다. 사용자 등 신뢰된 관측과 외부 도구 출력의 출처를 구분해 메모리에 저장하고, 역할별 질의와 결과 기반으로 학습한 보정 값을 이용해 행동을 선택한다. 연구진은 네 가지 에이전트 보안 과제에서 보안성과 유용성을 동시에 더 잘 달성한 기준선은 없었으며, SkillsBench와 ToolSafe에서 가장 강한 기준선 대비 F1이 각각 13.84점과 7.07점 높았다고 보고했다. 외부 입력이 위험한 행동으로 이어지는 것을 막으면서 정상 업무 수행을 보존하려는 접근으로, 보고된 효과의 범위는 평가 과제에 한정된다.

articles.title: Factorization-Guided Training and Inference for Diffusion-Drafted Speculative Decoding
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.23935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through parallel verification of tokens proposed by a drafter. Diffusion drafters further parallelize proposal generation, but greater proposal capacity or higher mean accepted tokens (MAT) need not yield higher throughput. Because verification accepts only a consecutive prefix, early rejections can render later correct predictions ineffective, limiting MAT gains, while even higher MAT may not improve throughput if per-round latency increases. We introduce DScout, which uses two complementary factorizations to guide diffusion drafter training and inference for higher throughput. For training, DScout factorizes position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction loss. This guides the design and combination of mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss to align supervision with prefix acceptance and improve MAT. For inference, DScout factorizes throughput as the ratio of MAT to per-round latency, guiding target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and inference block size selection to identify a high-throughput configuration for each workload. Across six benchmarks, DScout achieves $3.84\times$ and $4.14\times$ mean speedups over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, respectively, improving mean speedup over the state-of-the-art baseline by 9.1% and 7.1%. Across models and concurrency settings, our inference configuration policy provides up to 9.75% additional mean speedup over DScout's fixed configuration.
articles.summary: DScout는 확산 모델이 여러 토큰을 제안하고 대상 LLM이 병렬 검증하는 추측 디코딩의 학습과 실행 구성을 함께 최적화한다. 앞부분의 거절이 뒤쪽의 정확한 예측까지 무효화할 수 있다는 점을 반영해 학습 손실을 조정하고, 승인 토큰 수와 라운드 지연의 비율을 기준으로 추론 구성을 선택한다. 여섯 벤치마크에서 Qwen3‑4B와 Qwen3‑8B의 자기회귀 디코딩 대비 평균 3.84배와 4.14배 가속을 보고했으며, 기존 최상위 기준선 대비 평균 가속 배율 개선은 각각 9.1%와 7.1%였다. 제안 토큰의 정확도만 높이기보다 실제 처리량을 직접 고려해야 한다는 점에서 LLM 서빙 최적화에 실용적이다.

articles.title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.27027v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems improve performance on clinical tasks, and that improvement is often read as evidence of a more trustworthy system. However, the two are not the same claim. A clinician acts on the stated reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so whether collaboration reduces hallucination, and what decides when it does, has to be measured in the reasoning too. Yet most evaluations score only the final answer. We evaluate four systems (a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies) across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring hallucination, under a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy, inside the rationale each system generates and reporting it alongside the task metric. We report that collaboration buys task performance but not lower hallucination as a rule, and no topology is reliably better than another. The effect differs by model: of the $36$ model--system--task comparisons, $12$ are large enough to resolve --- four decreases and eight increases, with no model on both sides. What sets the level, and the direction of any change, is the model rather than the topology or the number of agents. A self-correction experiment is consistent with this: shown its own flagged errors, every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination; the one model for which collaboration lowers hallucination gains the most, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the model whose hallucination it amplifies most, does not reduce its hallucination at all. We find that collaboration redistributes what its models can already do; it does not supply what they cannot.
articles.summary: 임상 과제에서 다중 에이전트 협업이 최종 성능을 높여도 추론 설명의 환각을 일관되게 줄이지는 않는다는 연구가 나왔다. 연구진은 네 모델과 세 임상 과제에서 단일 모델 및 세 협업 구조를 비교했으며, 36개 비교 중 변화를 구분할 만큼 효과가 컸던 12개는 환각 감소 4개와 증가 8개로 나뉘었다. 환각 변화는 에이전트 수나 연결 구조보다 기반 모델에 더 크게 좌우됐고, 자체 오류를 알려준 뒤 수정하는 능력도 모델마다 달랐다. 의료 AI를 평가할 때 정답률 상승을 신뢰성 향상으로 간주하지 말고 설명 내부의 사실성과 충실성을 별도로 측정해야 함을 시사한다.

articles.title: MedPAO-Assist: Edge-Deployable, Modality-Aware Agentic AI for Radiology Report Structuring
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.26913v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models for radiology report structuring has been largely dominated by either proprietary cloud-based models or large open models requiring high-end GPUs for deployment, which is a critical bottleneck for clinical adoption in radiology workflows that demand data privacy and offline operation. To address this, we present MedPAO-Assist, an edge-deployable agentic framework that generates structured radiology reports directly from radiologist dictation and voice commands, requiring only $\approx3.3$ GB peak RAM and achieving an average end-to-end latency of $\approx31$ seconds on a standard laptop CPU through an asynchronous, multi-threaded execution pipeline. The system currently supports four major imaging modalities -- Chest X-ray, Chest CT, Abdomen CT, and Brain MRI. To our knowledge, it is among the earliest agentic systems to run its entire pipeline with a Small Language Model (SLM) in the 0.6B-parameter range. This multi-agent architecture, built around an Extract-Ground-Generate paradigm, performs concept extraction, SNOMED-CT grounding, and structured report generation, followed by a speech-driven human-in-the-loop correction phase, together forming a fully "no-touch" reporting workflow that requires no keyboard input, external API calls, or internet connectivity. We evaluate each pipeline stage individually -- concept extraction, ontology grounding, and concept categorization and report hardware profiling results demonstrating the system's feasibility for real-time, CPU-only clinical deployment.
articles.summary: MedPAO‑Assist는 방사선 전문의의 구술과 음성 명령을 구조화된 영상의학 보고서로 변환하는 오프라인 에이전트 프레임워크다. 약 6억 파라미터의 소형 언어모델을 중심으로 개념 추출, SNOMED‑CT 연결, 보고서 생성과 음성 수정 단계를 구성하며 흉부 X선·흉부 CT·복부 CT·뇌 MRI를 지원한다. 연구진은 일반 노트북 CPU에서 최대 RAM 약 3.3GB와 평균 종단 간 지연 약 31초를 보고했다. 외부 API 없이 민감한 임상 데이터를 처리할 가능성을 보여주지만, 제시된 평가는 파이프라인 단계와 하드웨어 실행 가능성 중심이며 임상 안전성을 입증한 것은 아니다.

articles.title: CrossFit-GS: Out-of-Fold Pose Estimation for COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting
articles.content: Pose-free 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) aims to bypass cumbersome Structure-from-Motion (SfM) by directly reconstructing scenes from unposed image sequences. In this work, we present CrossFit-GS, a deferred-commitment progressive framework that mitigates cumulative trajectory drift and breaks the self-reinforcing loop of distorted-map error propagation. Specifically, we partition the input sequence into interleaved subsets and maintain two complementary submaps. Each candidate pose is cross-refined against a frozen opposite submap that has never been optimized using the target frame, thereby providing an independent geometric reference for pose estimation. Checkerboard validation and spatial coverage safeguards further reject unreliable updates, and only verified poses are committed to their corresponding owner submap. Once the trajectory has been refined, the intermediate submaps are discarded and the final global representation is trained from scratch using the fixed refined poses. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that CrossFit-GS substantially reduces cumulative trajectory drift and consistently improves both camera pose estimation and novel-view synthesis over existing methods.
articles.summary: CrossFit‑GS는 사전 카메라 자세 추정 없이 이미지 시퀀스로 3D Gaussian Splatting 장면을 복원할 때 누적되는 궤적 오차를 줄이는 방법이다. 입력을 교차 배치된 두 부분집합으로 나눠 상보적 지도를 만들고, 각 프레임의 자세를 해당 프레임으로 학습하지 않은 반대쪽 고정 지도에 맞춰 검증한다. 신뢰할 수 있는 자세만 확정한 뒤 중간 지도를 버리고 전체 표현을 새로 학습해 잘못된 지도와 자세가 서로 오류를 강화하는 문제를 완화한다. 여러 벤치마크에서 자세 추정과 새 시점 합성 개선을 보고해, COLMAP 같은 사전 처리에 대한 의존도를 낮추는 3D 복원 워크플로에 활용 가능성을 제시한다.
